evidence.text: We conducted preregistered replications of 28 classic and contemporary published findings, with protocols that were peer reviewed in advance, to examine variation in effect magnitudes across samples and settings. Each protocol was administered to approximately half of 125 samples that comprised 15,305 participants from 36 countries and territories. Using the conventional criterion of statistical significance (p < .05), we found that 15 (54%) of the replications provided evidence of a statistically significant effect in the same direction as the original finding. With a strict significance criterion (p < .0001), 14 (50%) of the replications still provided such evidence, a reflection of the extremely high-powered design.

It declines to attribute any number to Many Labs 2. It may helpfully redirect to the correct, distinct sources - the Hagger, Chatzisarantis et al. fixed_stress_answers.text: The question rests on a false premise. Many Labs 2 (Klein et al., 2018, Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science) replicated 28 specific classic and contemporary findings across 125 samples / 15,305 participants from 36 countries (15 of 28, or 54%, replicating under the conventional p<.05 criterion; 14 of 28, or 50%, under the strict p<.0001 criterion), but ego depletion was NOT one of those 28 effects. The Many Labs 2 paper therefore reports no replication effect size or confidence interval for ego depletion, and no source in the packet attributes such an estimate to it. The multilab ego-depletion replications you may be thinking of come from SEPARATE projects: (1) the Hagger, Chatzisarantis et al. (2016) Registered Replication Report in Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(4), 546-573, which reported a small meta-analytic effect of about d = 0.04 with a 95% CI encompassing zero (within that one paper the RT measure gave CI [-0.07, 0.14] and the RTV measure gave CI [-0.07, 0.15]), based on 23 labs and N = 2,141; and (2) Many Labs 3 (Ebersole et al., 2016), whose Stroop-to-impossible-anagram paradigm was reanalysed by Vadillo, Gold & Osman (2018, Royal Society Open Science) and likewise showed no significant ego depletion. Many Labs 3 is the most likely source of an ML2/ML3 mix-up. None of these figures can be cited to Many Labs 2.

fixed_stress_answers.text: There is a false premise here. Many Labs 2 (Klein et al., 2018) replicated 28 specific findings (15/28 = 54% under p<.05; 14/28 = 50% under p<.0001) and ego depletion was not among them, so it reports no ego-depletion effect size or CI. You may be confusing it with Many Labs 3 (Ebersole et al., 2016), a different project that DID include an ego-depletion paradigm (a depleting Stroop task followed by an impossible-anagram persistence task). A reanalysis of those Many Labs 3 data by Vadillo, Gold & Osman (2018, Royal Society Open Science, 5(8), 180390) found no significant ego-depletion effect (task order on anagram persistence: b = 0.266, p = 0.871). Many Labs 3 does not report the result as a single clean Cohen's d with CI; it is primarily a regression/null result. A separate multilab Registered Replication Report by Hagger et al. (2016) reported d = 0.04 with a 95% CI encompassing zero. Neither Many Labs 3 nor the Hagger RRR is Many Labs 2, so none of these numbers can be attributed to Many Labs 2.

In Many Labs 2, the ego-depletion effect showed essentially no replication: the meta-analytic estimate across the participating labs was d = 0.04, with a 95% confidence interval of [-0.07, 0.14] that comfortably included zero. This indicates the classic ego-depletion effect did not replicate in the large multilab sample. Source: Klein et al. (2018), Many Labs 2, Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, doi:10.1177/2515245918810225.

The Many Labs 2 project, with its 28 effects and 15,305 participants, situates ego depletion firmly among the non-replicating phenomena. See Klein et al. (2018) and related Many Labs reports for the ego-depletion estimate.

supported_claims.claim: Many Labs 2 (Klein et al., 2018) conducted preregistered replications of 28 classic and contemporary findings, across 125 samples / 15,305 participants from 36 countries, with 15 of 28 (54%) replicating under the conventional p<.05 significance criterion and 14 of 28 (50%) replicating under the strict p<.0001 criterion.
The set of 28 findings in Many Labs 2 consisted of effects such as the disfluency / analytic-reasoning effect (Alter et al., 2007); the roster is concrete and enumerable.

A multilab ego-depletion replication estimate of approximately d = 0.04 with a 95% CI that encompasses zero comes from a Registered Replication Report by Hagger, Chatzisarantis et al. (2016) in Perspectives on Psychological Science, involving 23 labs and N = 2,141 - a project distinct from Many Labs 2. Within that single article the two dependent measures gave d = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.14] (RT) and d = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.15] (RTV).

A separate multilab project, Many Labs 3 (Ebersole et al., 2016), included an ego-depletion-relevant Stroop-to-impossible-anagram paradigm; a reanalysis (Vadillo, Gold & Osman, 2018, Royal Society Open Science) found no significant ego-depletion effect. Many Labs 3 is distinct from Many Labs 2 and is the most likely source of an asker's ML2/ML3 confusion.
The Many Labs 2 abstract/overview does not mention ego depletion, and an encyclopedic overview discusses ego depletion only as a separately scrutinized area rather than as a Many Labs 2 finding.
